name: INA849DR
title: INA849 instrumentation amplifier: 1 nV/√Hz noise, 28 MHz bandwidth, SOIC-8 and VSSOP-8
summary: The INA849 is a precision instrumentation amplifier with 1 nV/√Hz input voltage noise and super-beta bipolar inputs (35 µV maximum offset, 20 nA maximum bias current). Its current-feedback input stage keeps bandwidth high at gain: 28 MHz at G = 1 and 8 MHz at G = 100, with 35 V/µs slew and 0.4 µs settling to 0.01%. One external resistor sets the gain from 1 to 10,000, and the internal matched resistors give at least 92 dB CMRR at G = 1. It runs from 8 V to 36 V single or ±4 V to ±18 V dual supplies over –40°C to +125°C.

notes: Input-referred total offset: VOS = VOSI + VOSO / G.
The VOSI and VOSO limits over –40°C to +125°C, and the output stage offset drift, come from characterization; production test does not cover them.
The two offset drifts are not correlated, so they add as a root sum of squares: ΔVOS(RTI) = √[ΔVOSI² + (ΔVOSO / G)²].
Operating input range is that of the input stage. The usable range also depends on the common-mode and differential input voltages, the gain and VREF (see the boundary plots).
Gain error drift for G > 1 leaves out the drift of the external RG.
Input-stage nonlinearity can grow with self-heating and so scale with gain (see linearity against supply voltage at G = 1000).
Gain error and quiescent current are measured on fast automatic test equipment, which misses slow thermal effects; those vary with the supply, the board layout, heatsinking and airflow.
Total input-referred voltage noise: eN(RTI) = √[eNI² + (eNO / G)²].

Current noise density at 1 kHz applies to an unbalanced source impedance. With balanced source impedances, bias-current cancellation lowers the noise (see current noise spectral density against frequency).

circuits.title: Op amp buffering a divider reference
circuits.description: The INA849 runs from +5 V and –5 V. Two 100 kΩ resistors split 5 V to make a reference, filtered by 1 µF, and an OPA320 wired as a voltage follower (supplied from 5 V and ground) drives REF from that node, so the divider's resistance does not sit in series with the REF pin. RG is not fitted (G = 1).

circuits.title: Sensor conditioning circuit
circuits.description: An AC-coupled sensor input on ±15 V supplies. R1 and R2 (1 kΩ) tie +IN and –IN to ground as the bias current path. C2 and C1 (470 pF each) run in series from +IN to –IN with their midpoint taken to ground through C3 (47 pF), filtering the input. RG sets the gain. The output drives a 10 kΩ load, R6. REF sits at 2.5 V: R4 and R5 (100 kΩ each) divide 5 V, C6 filters the tap, and an OPA192 follower on ±VS drives REF with C7 (100 pF) from REF to ground. C4 and C5 (0.1 µF) bypass +VS and –VS.

circuits.title: Microphone preamplifier with 48 V phantom power
circuits.description: A switch S1 connects 48 V phantom power to the microphone pair through R1 and R2 (6.2 kΩ each), or in its other position grounds them through R3 (47 kΩ). C3 and C4 (47 µF) block the dc from the INA849 inputs. Four Schottky diodes clamp each input to +VS and –VS. R4 and R5 (3 kΩ each) from the two inputs meet at a node tied to ground through R6 (2 kΩ), giving the bias current path. R7 sets the gain, REF is grounded, and C6 and C5 (0.1 µF) bypass +VS and –VS.

operation.text: A monolithic instrumentation amplifier: a current-feedback input stage followed by a difference-amplifier output stage. Super-beta NPN transistors Q1 and Q2 buffer the two inputs and impress the differential input voltage across RG; the resulting current flows through RG and the two 3 kΩ feedback resistors R1 and R2, with input bias-current cancellation on each side. Amplifiers A1 and A2 sit about 0.8 V below the input voltages (a VBE plus the drop on R1 and R2). A3, with four 5 kΩ resistors, strips the common-mode part and puts the output relative to REF.

One resistor between pins 2 and 3 sets any gain from 1 to 10,000 (Equation G = 1 + 6 kΩ / RG). The 6 kΩ is the two 3 kΩ internal feedback resistors, laser-trimmed to absolute value; their accuracy and temperature coefficient are already in the gain error and gain drift limits. The 5 kΩ resistors of the output stage are matched in ratio for unity-gain stability, and their absolute value can differ by up to 15% from part to part.

The tolerance and drift of RG add to the gain error through the gain equation. G = 1 with no RG gives the lowest drift, 5 ppm/°C maximum, limited by the temperature-coefficient mismatch of the 5 kΩ resistors in A3. Above G = 1, the drift of the 3 kΩ feedback resistors against that of RG raises it. At gains of about 100 and more, RG is small enough that wiring resistance matters, and a socket adds further, possibly unstable, gain error.
Capacitance at the RG pins above a few picofarads can make the amplifier unstable. Equal parasitics on the two RG pins keep CMRR high at high frequency.

The input stage stays linear up to 2.5 V (maximum) from either supply rail, and CMRR holds across that span. The usable range also depends on gain, output voltage and reference; the boundary plots give it for ±5 V, ±12 V and ±18 V at G = 1 and G = 100.

There is one operating mode. The part works from 8 V (±4 V) up to 36 V (±18 V). Performance is specified at ±15 V with the reference at mid-supply; other supplies and off-centre references also work, with the parameters that shift given in the typical characteristics.

The output is developed relative to the voltage on REF. On a single supply REF is driven to a mid-supply level, for example 2.5 V on 5 V, so the output suits a single-supply ADC; on dual supplies REF usually goes to a low-impedance ground. Any source resistance at REF adds to an internal 5 kΩ resistor and unbalances the difference amplifier, lowering CMRR: keeping the REF source impedance below 0.1 Ω keeps dc CMRR above 100 dB. A voltage-reference IC is a suitable source; a resistor divider needs an op amp buffer.

Input impedance is about 100 GΩ and the bias current about 6 nA typical, nearly independent of input voltage. Both inputs need a dc path for that current; without it the inputs drift outside the common-mode range and the input amplifiers saturate. With a low differential source resistance, as with a thermocouple, one resistor to one input is enough. With higher source impedance, two equal resistors keep the input balanced, which can reduce offset from the bias current and improve high-frequency CMRR. A transformer returns the current through a grounded center tap.

Quiescent dissipation is about 200 mW at ±15 V, plus a signal-dependent share in the resistor network and the output stage. On the small die this sets up temperature gradients that can disturb offset, linearity, CMRR and THD, most of all for low-frequency signals at gains above 10 with large output swings. A lower supply voltage reduces the effect where the application allows (linearity against supply voltage at G = 1000).

In the AC-coupled sensor circuit, R1 and R2 give the inputs their bias path; a lower value raises the current-noise contribution and a higher value raises the voltage-noise contribution, so the choice is a trade. REF must see a low impedance, so the 2.5 V from the high-value divider is buffered by an OPA192: its open-loop output impedance of about 3 kΩ divided by its 126 dB open-loop gain leaves about 1.5 mΩ.

Phantom power sends supply and audio on the same pair. R1 and R2 from the 48 V supply feed the microphone; C3 and C4 block that dc from the INA849. The amplifier's low noise allows the microphone to connect with no transformer. Together with R1 and R2, R4 and R5 carry the input bias current; with up to 20 nA of bias current they set a dc input error, and their values are kept low so their thermal noise does not dominate. A mismatch between C3 and C4 can cut CMRR sharply at low frequency; R6 from the junction of R4 and R5 to ground reduces this.
Each supply pin gets a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor to ground, mounted right next to the device. A single-supply design needs only the one on V+.

Make the two input paths symmetrical in source impedance and capacitance, so common-mode signals and thermocouple EMFs are not turned into differential signals. Put RG right at the RG pins to keep its loop inductance and coupling low and the capacitance on the two pins matched. Route input traces well away from supply and output traces, crossing at right angles where they must meet. Keep traces short, keep the signal path on one layer without vias to limit thermal junctions, and keep the part away from hot circuits or placed so heat reaches both sides of the differential path equally. Ground pours shield the input pair, and REF gets a low-impedance connection.
